clinicalPearls: Defined by an early repolarisation ECG pattern (J-point elevation or notching/slurring at the QRS-ST junction) in the inferior and/or lateral leads together with documented ventricular arrhythmia or resuscitated cardiac arrest
The early repolarisation ECG pattern alone is common and usually benign; the syndrome label requires an associated malignant arrhythmic event
Considered one of the J-wave syndromes, sharing mechanistic overlap with Brugada syndrome
Higher-risk features include marked J-point elevation, a horizontal or descending ST segment, and inferior or global lead distribution
Typically presents in young to middle-aged adults, often men, with syncope or aborted sudden death, sometimes during sleep or at rest
Most cases are sporadic, but familial clustering occurs and variants in cardiac ion-channel genes have been described in a minority
Diagnosis is one of exclusion after structural heart disease and other channelopathies have been ruled out
reference.pathophysiology: Early repolarisation syndrome is thought to arise from heterogeneity in the early phases of the ventricular action potential, particularly an accentuated transient outward potassium current relative to inward currents in the epicardium. This creates a voltage gradient across the ventricular wall that produces the characteristic J-point elevation on the ECG and, when pronounced, favours phase-2 re-entry and closely coupled ventricular ectopy that can trigger polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. The tendency is modulated by autonomic tone, explaining events at rest or during sleep. A subset of patients carry variants in genes controlling these ionic currents, placing the disorder among the inherited J-wave syndromes, though for most individuals no single causal gene is identified.
additionalDifferentials: Benign early repolarisation pattern without arrhythmia
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG characterising J-point elevation morphology and distribution
Ambulatory and event monitoring to capture arrhythmia
Echocardiography and cardiac MRI to exclude structural disease
Coronary assessment to exclude ischaemia in appropriate patients
Genetic testing and family screening in selected high-risk or familial cases
Exclusion of other channelopathies including drug-provocation testing where indicated
redFlags: Resuscitated cardiac arrest or documented polymorphic ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation
Unexplained syncope with a high-risk early repolarisation pattern
Family history of sudden unexplained death at a young age
Marked J-point elevation with a horizontal or descending ST segment
reference.prognosis: The isolated ECG pattern carries a very low absolute risk, whereas the full syndrome with a prior malignant arrhythmic event confers a meaningful risk of recurrence; risk stratification and secondary prevention, including defibrillator therapy in survivors of cardiac arrest, guide outcome.
pitfalls: Labelling every early repolarisation ECG pattern as dangerous and causing undue alarm
Missing higher-risk morphological features when assessing an early repolarisation ECG
Confusing the pattern with pericarditis or ischaemia
Failing to exclude structural disease and other channelopathies before diagnosing the syndrome
references: ESC guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death
management: Implant a cardioverter-defibrillator for secondary prevention in survivors of aborted sudden death or documented ventricular arrhythmia
Infuse isoprenaline for acute electrical storm and use quinidine for chronic arrhythmia suppression
Consider catheter ablation targeting triggering ventricular ectopy for refractory arrhythmia
Risk-stratify using ECG features such as marked J-point elevation, a horizontal or descending ST segment and inferior or global lead distribution
Reassure and avoid overtreating the common benign isolated early repolarisation pattern
Offer genetic testing and cascade family screening in high-risk or familial cases
Exclude structural disease, ischaemia and other channelopathies, including drug-provocation testing where indicated
Refer to a specialist inherited cardiac conditions clinic
